Attainment and Attendance in Rother

What the national model behind How to Pull the Right Lever says about the district’s secondary schools, within East Sussex and alongside Brighton and Hove. Draft for discussion.

Author
Affiliation

Adam Dennett

Bartlett Centre for Advanced Spatial Analysis, University College London

Published

October 31, 2026

WarningDraft for discussion

One of the district documents for Sussex. It sits beneath the East Sussex document, and the district summary compares all of the districts. Every figure comes from published Department for Education data and the national models of How to Pull the Right Lever. Nothing uses pupil-level records. The commentary is written to a common pattern from the figures; read it as a starting point for discussion.

Summary

Rother’s results are below the middle of England’s districts, on an intake less disadvantaged than England’s. Its 5 state secondary schools are in Battle, Bexhill-on-Sea, Robertsbridge and Rye.

  • Overall results: 45.4 in Attainment 8 in 2024/25, 153rd of 264 districts in England.
  • Disadvantage: 25.6% of pupils are disadvantaged, against 28.3% nationally.
  • Disadvantaged pupils average 34.5, below the national 37.8 (193rd of 264).
  • The gap between disadvantaged pupils and the rest is 14.6 points, the 66th widest of 264.

The other findings:

  • For all pupils, Rother is 1.5 points below England. The largest pieces in the national model are Ofsted ratings (-0.8) and absence (-0.7). The district’s schools do about what the model expects.
  • For disadvantaged pupils it is 3.0 points below England. The largest pieces are being in the South East (-1.3) and English as an additional language (-1.0), and the schools add 0.3 points beyond what the model expects.
  • No district effect can be found. Once intake, East Sussex’s county effect and the schools themselves are accounted for, nothing is left that all Rother schools share.
  • 2 of the 5 schools are above expectation over 2021/22 to 2024/25. The strongest is St Richard’s Catholic College (+3.9); the weakest Bexhill High Academy (-1.6).
  • Absence was 8.0% in autumn and spring 2025/26 (8.4% a year earlier), against 8.0% for England and 8.9% for East Sussex. Over 2021/22 to 2024/25 its schools ran 0.1 points above what their intakes predict, and Rye College and Robertsbridge Community College more than a point above.
  • Reduced timetables run at 1.1 times the national rate, and suspensions at 0.8 times (17.1 per 100 pupils, against 21.2).
  • Disadvantaged groups are small, 32 to 96 pupils a year per school. Every school-level figure for them moves from year to year and should be read over several years.

1 About this analysis

Rother is a district of East Sussex, not a local authority, and that shapes what can be said:

  • The national models place schools in local authorities. The “local authority effect” in this document is East Sussex’s, shared with every school in the county.
  • What is particular to Rother shows up in its schools’ own residuals, and in the district test of Section 6.
  • Absence and exclusions are summed over the district’s 5 schools, followed through any change of URN.

The methods are described in full in the East Sussex document.

4 What explains attainment in Rother

The decomposition for Rother, in Attainment 8 points. ‘Place’ is East Sussex’s effect plus the South East’s; ‘unexplained’ is what the district’s own schools add beyond everything the model accounts for.

For all pupils, Rother is 1.5 points below England. The pieces of at least a quarter of a point:

  • Ofsted ratings (-0.80);
  • absence (-0.69);
  • prior attainment (+0.47);
  • being in the South East (-0.46);
  • East Sussex’s county-wide effect (+0.46);
  • English as an additional language (-0.36);
  • the teacher workforce (-0.35);
  • and the district’s schools themselves (-0.03), beyond what the model expects.

For disadvantaged pupils, Rother is 3.0 points below England. The pieces of at least a quarter of a point:

  • being in the South East (-1.32);
  • English as an additional language (-0.98);
  • absence (-0.75);
  • Ofsted ratings (-0.72);
  • prior attainment (+0.42);
  • admissions (-0.30);
  • East Sussex’s county-wide effect (+0.29);
  • and the district’s schools themselves (+0.30), beyond what the model expects.

5 The disadvantaged gap, school by school

No Rother school is above expectation for its non-disadvantaged pupils while more than a point below it for its disadvantaged ones. Claverham Community College and St Richard’s Catholic College are above expectation for both groups. The table below gives each school’s own persistent effect, from the model with a school term, which is the steadier measure.

6 Is there a Rother effect?

The district test of the East Sussex document adds a district level to the national model, with and without each school’s own record.

None of Rother’s district effects can be told apart from zero on either specification. The district’s results are explained by its intake, East Sussex’s county effect and its individual schools.

7 Absence

  • 8.0% absence in autumn and spring 2025/26, against 8.0% for England and 8.9% for East Sussex. A year earlier it was 8.4%.
  • Persistent absence is 21.9%, against 21.6% for England.
  • Against its intake, the district’s schools run 0.14 points above what their pupils’ profiles predict, on average over 2021/22 to 2024/25.
  • Rye College and Robertsbridge Community College each run more than a point above their predicted absence.
  • Claverham Community College and St Richard’s Catholic College run more than a point below their predictions.

Reduced timetables account for 0.34% of sessions, against 0.29% in England, 1.1 times the national rate. Robertsbridge Community College’s rate is the highest in the district.

3 of the 5 schools are above the national average absence in 2024/25. Bringing them to it would add up to 3.2 points for all pupils, as an indication of scale.

Suspensions were 17.1 per 100 pupils in 2024/25, against 21.2 for England and 28.0 for East Sussex.

9 Questions for discussion

  1. Disadvantaged pupils. They average 34.5 in Rother against 37.8 in England, and the district’s schools add 0.3 points for them beyond what the model expects. What do St Richard’s Catholic College and Claverham Community College, above expectation for these pupils, do that the district’s other schools could share?
  2. Attendance is a modest lever. Absence costs the district 0.7 points against England for all pupils, and Rye College and Robertsbridge Community College run more than a point above what their intakes predict.
  3. Schools, not the place. There is no Rother district effect: the differences that matter are between its schools.
  4. Practice. Reduced timetables and suspensions are close to or below the national rate.
  5. The county. East Sussex’s own effect for disadvantaged pupils is +0.9% (60th of 151), not distinguishable from zero. The county questions in the East Sussex document apply here as well.

Notes on method

Methods and sources are those of the East Sussex document. District membership comes from each school’s postcode (ONS postcode directory, via postcodes.io). Absence and exclusions for the district are summed over its schools, including any predecessor or successor URNs. This document is generated from templates/district_report.qmd by R/20_district_reports.R, from data built by R/17_area_analysis.R, R/18_district_effects.R and R/19_trust_effects.R. Its format is described in AREA_REPORTS.md.
